vignette: Anika sits on the edge of the therapist’s sofa, her hands folded tightly over her knees. At forty-two, she has spent the better part of two decades cleaning other people’s spaces, and the habit of scanning rooms hasn’t left her. When she enters this office, her eyes track the windows, the door handle, the placement of the chairs. She arranges her bag on the floor beside her feet, always with the strap looped around her ankle. “I used to just work,” she says, her voice quiet but steady. “Now I count my steps. I count the lights. I count the breaths between sirens.” Three years ago, during a humid summer in her home neighborhood, a former colleague begins leaving notes in the stairwell of her building. At first, the messages are polite, almost polite in their precision about her schedule. Then they shift. She finds gloves identical to hers taped under the stair railing. A photograph of her own kitchen window arrives in her mailbox, taken from the street below. When she shows them to her husband, Ravi, they go to the police together. The officer files a report, warns the man, and tells her to rest easy. But the silence after the station is worse than the noise. The notes return. They appear on her windshield. Under her door. Taped to the back of Ravi’s office chair. Anika stops trusting deadbolts. She sleeps on the floor beside Ravi’s bed, a baseball bat wrapped in electrical tape beneath the mattress. She changes the routes she takes to job sites, waking at 3 a.m. to check weather apps, then neighborhood watch groups, then the lock on her suitcase. Work becomes a performance. She accepts only cleaning assignments in homes with security cameras, thick curtains, and neighbors who wave through windows. But even there, she finds herself pausing mid-swipe, listening to the hum of the refrigerator, imagining the scrape of boots on tile behind her. She deletes her social media. She lets unknown numbers ring into voicemail. When her employer calls about her sporadic attendance, she tells him she’s unwell, though her body feels fine except for the constant tightening in her chest, the way her jaw locks when a car backfires. Ravi tries to hold her when the nights grow heavy, but Anika stiffens at the first touch. She doesn’t want him to know she flinches at his footsteps in the hallway, or that she measures his distance across the room like she’s calculating an exit. Their conversations have shrunk to logistics: grocery lists, utility bills, the price of bus fare. She still cooks his meals, still folds his shirts, but the gestures feel mechanical now, like she’s replaying a version of her life that no longer exists. When she speaks, she often stops mid-sentence, waiting for a sound that isn’t there. “I know he’s not here,” she tells me during our fifth session. “But my body doesn’t. My body is still waiting for the door to open.” She leaves the office with the same careful routine: bag on the floor, strap around her wrist, three steps back before the door clicks shut behind her. Outside, the city moves at its usual pace, but Anika walks slightly ahead of the crowd, eyes fixed on the pavement, shoulders pulled inward. She still cleans houses. She still loves her husband. She still wonders, every time the phone rings, whether this is the call that changes everything again.
